scene: Child: (standing up, looking curious and slightly distracted)
Parent: "W E L C O M E"
Child: (starts looking at wristbands, not fully engaged with the tablet)
Child: (still looking at wristbands, slightly puzzled)
Parent: "Oh, M?"
Child: (nodding, still focused on wristbands, begins to adjust them)
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: "M"
Parent: "Oh we can't, we can't [inaudible 00:00:12] we have to do that."
Child: (continues fidgeting with wristbands)
Child: (points at the wristbands, looking thoughtful)
Parent: "Why does it say left and right?"
Child: (glances briefly at the parent, then back at wristbands)
Child: (continues to fiddle with wristbands, appearing focused)
Parent: "Foreign Language (Hebrew)"
Child: (nods while still concentrating on the wristbands)
Child: (looking at the tablet, not engaging with the parent)
Parent: So now I will tell you how to use our story reading app. It's here.
Child: Ooh.
Parent: There are two types of stories. Short stories are about five minutes long, and long stories are between five to ten minutes.
Child: (looking more closely at the tablet)
Parent: Okay. So for example, if you choose a short story—[crosstalk].
Child: Oh, we know those.
Parent: You will have to find types of [inaudible].
Child: Ahhh.
Parent: Okay, so swipe to see more.
Child: Okay.
Parent: Once you choose one, you can click this corner to go to the next page. You can also click this corner to go to the previous page.
Child: (leaning over the tablet, touching the screen)
Parent: Okay, once the book is open I can.
Child: (continues touching the screen)
Child: (focused on the tablet)
Parent: Also, there will be two buttons you can click to go back to bookshelf or to go back to first page.
Child: (nods, looks at screen)
Child: (leans closer to the tablet)
Parent: Okay.
Child: I read this book by myself. It's really long.
Child: (points at the screen)
Parent: Do you want to see what the long stories are?
Child: Yeah.
Child: (looking at the screen with interest)
Parent: You will be reading the stories for 20 minutes.
Child: (nods)
Child: (engaged with the tablet, eyes on the screen)
Parent: Okay, so we just pick one and we start reading?
Child: (nods, still looking at the screen)
Child: (holding the tablet, preparing to start reading)
Parent: (observing and ready to assist)
Child: (focused on the tablet)
(Parent and child are now engaged in reading the story on the tablet together, with the facilitator moving away)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "[crosstalk 00:01:34] Should we start?"
Child: (looking at the tablet, pointing at the page)
Parent: "Once upon a time there was a little house, way out in the country. She was a pretty little house, and she was strong and well built."
Child: (looking at the tablet, tapping on the screen)
Parent: "How do we go to the next page? Maybe on the screen, ooh there."
Child: (looking at the tablet, listening)

Parent: "The man who built her so well said 'This little house shall never be sold for gold or silver, and she will live to see our great great grandchildren's; great great grandchildren living in her.'"
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: "The little house was very happy, and she sat on the hill and watched the countryside around her. She watched the sun rise in the morning, and she watched the sun set in the evening. Day followed day, each one a little different from the one before but the little house stayed just the same."
Child: (focused on the tablet and pointing at the screen)
Parent: "In the nights she watched the moon grow from a thin new moon to a full moon. Then back again to a thin old moon, and when there was no moon, she watched the stars."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, seemingly engaged)
Parent: "Way off in the distance she could see the lights of the city. The little house was curious about the city and wondered what it would be like to live there."
Child: (continues to look at the screen while the parent reads)

Parent: "Time passed quickly for the little house as she watched the countryside slowly change with the seasons. In the spring, when the days grew longer and the sun warmer, she waited for the first robin to return from the south."
Child: (looks up and asks a question)
Parent: "What's a robin Leo? It's a little bird."
Child: (returns attention to the tablet)
Parent: "She watched the grass turn green, she watched the buds on the trees swell and the apple trees burst into blossom. She watched the children playing in the brook."
Child: (curious and engaged, continues looking at the screen)
Parent: "Do you know what the brook is?"
Child: (looking at the tablet, focused on the story)
Parent: "No."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, focused on the story)
Parent: "It's a little river."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, focused on the story)

Parent: "In the long summer days, she sat in the sun and watched the trees cover themselves with leaves and the white daisie's cover the hills. She watched the gardens grow and she watched the apples turn red and ripen. She watched the children swimming in the pool."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, focused on the story)
Parent: "In the fall when days grew shorter and the nights colder, she watched the first frost turn the leaves to bright yellow and orange and red."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, focused on the story)
Parent: "Do you know what frost is? It's sort of ice that comes."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, focused on the story)
Parent: "She watched the harvest gathered and the apples picked. She watched the children going back to school."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, focused on the story)
Parent: "What's this? Is that winter?"
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: (turning head to look at parent, then back at the tablet)

Parent: "In the winter, when the nights were long, and the days were short, and the countryside covered with snow, she watched the children coasting and skating. Year followed year, the apples trees grew old, and new ones were planted. The children grew up and went away to the city, and now at night the lights of the city seemed brighter and closer."
Child: (holding the side of the head with one hand, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "One day, the little house was surprised to see a horseless carriage coming down the winding country road."
Child: (holding the side of the head with one hand, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "What do you think that is? A horseless carriage?"
Child: (holding the side of the head with one hand, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "I don't know."
Child: (holding the side of the head with one hand, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "You think they came up with cars? Because, the time is passing."
Child: (looking at the tablet, engaged with the story)
Parent: "Pretty soon, there were more of them on the road and fewer carriages pulled by horses."
Child: (still engaged with the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, seemingly curious)
Parent: "What does that mean?"
Child: "That there were more cars and less horses pulled by...there was less cabins pulled by horses."
Child: (looking at the tablet, processing the information)
Parent: "Pretty soon along came some surveyors and surveyed a line in front of the little house. Pretty soon along came a steam shovel and dug a road through the hill covered with daisies."
Child: (focused on the tablet, contemplating the story)
Child: (still engaged, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Wow what do you think is happening?"
Child: "They're making into the city.[crosstalk 00:05:42]"
Child: (pointing at the screen)
Parent: They're making the roads? What did it look like before?[inaudible 00:05:47]
Child: I don't want too.
Parent: You don't want too?
Child: (continues to point at the screen)
Parent: Oh, look here there's a sled with a horse, and now they have roads coming.
Child: (leans in closer to the tablet)
Parent: Oh I see them.
Child: (continues to look and point at the tablet)
Parent: Ooh, sorry what did you say?
Child: I see boats.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Boats? Yeah, maybe. Okay here they're making rooms."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, starting to touch ear)

Parent: "Then some trucks came and dumped big stones on the road. Then some trucks with little stones, then some trucks with tar and sand, and finally a steam roller came and rolled it all smooth, and the road was done."
Child: (touches ear with right hand)
Child: (continues touching ear with right hand while looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Do you think here they're beginning and then here time goes by, now that they're making the road?"
Child: (starts to bend forward slightly, looking at the tablet)
Child: (leans forward, right hand still on ear)
Parent: "Look, the big pedals, small ones and this is the tar and the steam roller."
Child: (leans further forward, hands near the tablet)
Child: (glances at the tablet, right hand still touching ear)

Parent: "Now the little house watched the trucks and automobiles going back and forth to the city. Gasoline stations, roadside stands, and small houses followed the new road. Everyone and everything moved much faster now than before. More roads were made, and the country side was divided into lots. More houses and bigger houses, apartment houses, and tenant houses, school, stores, and garages spread over the land and crowded over the little house."
Child: (continues to touch ear)
Child: (leans slightly back from the tablet, still touching ear)

Parent: "No one wanted to live in her and take care of her anymore. She couldn't be sold for gold and silver, so she just stayed there and watched. Now it was not so quiet and peaceful at night. Now the lights of the city were bright and very close, and the streets lights shown all night."
Child: (continues looking at tablet, right hand near ear)
Child: (glances sideways briefly, then back to the tablet, right hand still near ear)
Parent: "This must be living in the city," thought the little house, and didn't know whether she liked it or not. Shed miss the feel of daisies and the apple trees dancing in the moonlight."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, right hand on ear)
Child: (leans back slightly, right hand near ear)

Parent: "Pretty soon there were trolley cars going in back and forth in front of the little house. They went back and forth all day and part of the night. Everyone seemed to be very busy and everyone seemed to be in a hurry. Pretty soon there was an elevator train going back and forth above the little house. The air was filled with dust and smoke and the nose was so loud that it shook the little house."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, right hand still near ear)
Child: (looking at the tablet, one hand resting on the chin)
Parent: You think we can add something else though?
Child: (raises hand to his mouth) Nahh.
Parent: (still pointing at the tablet) No, is it full?
Child: (drops hand and looks at the tablet)
Parent: (continues pointing at the tablet, head slightly tilted towards the child) Now she couldn't tell when spring came or summer or fall or winter. It all seemed about the same.
Child: (keeps looking at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, listening attentively)
Parent: "Ooh, you can go underneath."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, listening attentively)

Parent: "Pretty soon there was a subway going back and forth underneath the little house. She couldn't see it, but she could feel and hear it. People were moving faster and faster, no one noticed the little house anymore. They hurried by without a glance. Pretty soon they tore down the apartment houses and tenement houses around the little house and started digging big cellars, one on each side. The steam shovels dug down three stories on one side and four stories on the other side. Pretty soon they started building up. They built up 25 stories on one side and 35 stories on the other. Now the little house only saw the sun at noon and didn't see the moon or stars at night at all because the lights of the city were too bright. She didn't like living in the city."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, listening attentively)
Parent: "At night she used to dream of the country and the field of daisies and the apple tree dancing in the moonlight."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, listening attentively)
Parent: "How do you think this is going to end?"
Child: (looking at the parent, responding)
Parent: (listening to the child's response, "Um, In the end the person that named him.. that made him.. saw him.. the house.")
Child: (looking at the tablet again)
Parent: "Oh yeah? Have you seen this book before?"
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "The little house was very sad and lonely. The paint was cracked and dirty, her windows were broken and her shutters hung crookedly. She looked shabby. Though she was just as good a house just as ever underneath. In one fine morning in spring, along came the great great granddaughter of the man who had built the little house so well. She saw the shabby little house but she didn't hurry by. There was something about the little house that made her stop and look again."
Child: (sitting next to the parent, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "You think she's going to look there?"
Child: (sitting next to the parent, still looking at the tablet)

Parent: "She said to her husband, 'That little house looks just like a little house my grandmother lived in when she was a little girl. Only that little house was way out in the country on a hill covered with daises and apple trees growing around.' They found out it was the very same house, so they went to the movers to see if the little house could be moved."
Child: (sitting next to the parent, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "The movers looked the little house all over and said 'sure, this house is as good as ever, she's built so well can we move her anywhere.'"
Child: (sitting next to the parent, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "That looks like a good idea. Can you help with turning the page?"
Child: (leaning closer to the tablet, starting to interact with it)
Parent: "How do you draw on the line?"
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Ooh, there you go."
Child: (sitting close to the parent, resting their chin on their hand while looking at the tablet)

Parent: "So they jacked up the little house and put her on wheels. Traffic was held up for hours as they slowly moved her out of the city. At first the little house was frightened, but after she got used to it she rather liked it. They rolled along the big road and they rolled along the little roads. Until they were way out in the country."
Child: (gesturing towards the tablet with both hands)
Parent: "It says the time, so first the.. she was like that and then that and then that. Right?"
Child: (pointing at the tablet with their finger)
Parent: "That, That that that."
Child: (pointing at the tablet with one finger and looking at the parent)

Parent: "When the little house saw the green grass and heard the birds singing she didn't feel sad anymore. They went along and along but they couldn't seem to find just a right place. They tried the little house here, then they tried her there. Finally, they saw a little hill in the middle of a field and apple trees growing around."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Is that where they're going to put her?"
Child: (reading the tablet, leaning in)
Parent: "Thank you."
Child: (touching their lip, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "There." Said the great great granddaughter. “That is just the place.” “Yes, it is." Thought the little house to her herself. A cellar was dug on top of the hill and slowly removed the house from the road to the hill.
Child: (resting head on their hand, looking attentively at the tablet)
Parent: "The windows and shutters were fixed and once again they painted her a lovely shade of pink. As the little house settled down on a new foundation, she smiled happily."
Child: (resting head on hand, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "You think that's it? Sounds like the end of the book."
Child: (navigating on the tablet)
Parent: "You think that was it? How do you go back, maybe with the arrow?"
Child: (tapping on the tablet)
Parent: "Is there a book you haven't read yet?"
Child: (tapping on the screen, pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "I think I don't know this one."
Child: (holding an object and looking at their hands, not the tablet)
Parent: (looking at the tablet) "This one? The one evening after thinking it over for sometime, Harold decided to go for a walk in the moonlight."
Child: (takes the tablet from the parent and looks at it)
Parent: "Ooh, thank you."
Child: (holding the tablet, then goes back to looking at their hands)

Parent: "He made a long, straight path so he wouldn't get lost and set off on his walk, taking his big purple crayon with him. But he didn't seem to be getting anywhere on the long straight path. So he left the path for a shortcut across the field and the moon went with him. The shortcut led right to where Harold thought a forest ought to be. He didn't want to get lost in the woods so he made a very small forest with just one tree in it."
Child: (looking at the tablet, attentive)
Parent: (points at the tablet) "Is that a forest, Leo?"
Child: "No."
Parent: "Just one tree?"
Child: (nods or doesn't respond, remains attentive to the tablet)
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "It turned out to be an apple tree. 'The apple will be very tasty,' Harold thought when they got wet. So he put a frightened dragon under the tree to guard the apples."
Child: (listening attentively, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "It was a terribly frightening dragon. It even frightened Harold, he backed away. His hand holding the purple crayon shook. Suddenly he realized what was happening."
Child: (slightly curious expression, looking at the parent)
Parent: "What is happening?"
Child: (slightly smiling, looking at the parent)
Parent: "Water?"
Child: (smiling, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "He falls in it?"
Child: (looking at the tablet, focused)
Parent: "But by the Harold was over his head in an ocean. He came up thinking fast."
Child: (looking at the tablet, attentive)
Parent: "What is he thinking?"
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Making a vowel."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Is that a good idea?"
Child: (looking up and slightly smiling)
Parent: (glancing at the child)
Child: "Yeah."

Parent: (continuing to read from the tablet) "And in no time he was climbing aboard a trim little boat. He quickly set sail... and the moon sailed along with him. After he had sailed long enough Harold made land without much trouble."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Is that where you put an infant?"
Child: (smiling while looking at the tablet)
Child: "No."
Child: (looking at the parent, holding a small ball, and smiling)
Parent: "No."
Child: (looking at the tablet, with interest and focus)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "He stepped ashore on the beach wondering where he was. The sandy beach reminded Harold of picnics and the thoughts of picnics made him hungry."
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)
Child: (looks at the parent briefly and then at the tablet)
Parent: "Hungry"
Child: (seems to smile and shift slightly while looking at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, shifting the ball between hands)
Parent: "So he laid out a nice simple picnic lunch. There was nothing but pie."
Child: (appears intrigued, looking intently at the tablet)
Child: (still looking at the tablet, calm and focused)
Parent: "What would you want to have? Would you draw a pie?"
Child: (looks up at the parent, showing contemplation)
Child: (looks up at the parent, then back at the tablet)
Parent: "No."
Child: (shaking head slightly, maintaining eye contact with the parent momentarily)
Child: (looking at the tablet and back up at the parent)
Parent: "No, what would you draw?"
Child: (looks up at parent and answers confidently)
Child: "I would draw hotdogs."
Child: (smiling and looking up at the parent)
Parent: "Hotdogs? With chocolate on top?"
Child: (giggles and nods slightly)
Child: (focuses back on the tablet, still smiling)
Child: (looking up at the parent)
Parent: "No, it’s not [inaudible 00:16:31]"
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "But they were all nine types of pie that Harold liked best. When Harold finished his picnic there was quite a lot left."
Child: (looking at the parent)
Parent: "What is he doing?"
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Yeah. He hated to see so much delicious pie go to waste. So Harold left the very hungry moose and a deserving porcupine to finish it up. And off he went, looking for a hill to climb to see where he was. Harold knew that the higher up he went, the farther he could see. So he decided to make the hill into a?"
Child: (looking thoughtful)
Parent: "Mount?"
Child: (still looking thoughtful)
Parent: "Mountain."
Child: (nodding)
Parent: "Yeah. If he went high enough he thought he could see the window of his bedroom. What do you think?"
Child: (still looking at the tablet)

Parent: "He was tired and felt he ought to be getting to bed. He hoped he could see his bedroom window from the top of the mountain. But as he looked down over the other side he slipped. There was any other side of the mountain, he was falling in thin air. But luckily he kept his wits and his purple crayon."
Child: (looking at the parent)
Parent: "What did he do?"
Child: (smiling)
Parent: "Draw a balloon."
Child: (nodding)

Parent: "He made a balloon and he grabbed onto it. And he made a basket under the balloon big enough to stand in. He had a fine view from the balloon but he couldn't see his window, he couldn't even see a house. So, he made a house with windows. And he landed on the balloon on the grass in the front yard. None of the windows were his window. He tried to think where his window ought to be. He made some more windows. He made a big building full of windows. He made lots of buildings full of windows. He made a whole city full of windows. But none of the windows was his window."
Child: (listening)

Parent: "He couldn't think where it might be. He decided to ask a policeman. The policeman pointed the way Harold was going anyway but Harold thanked him. And he walked along with the moon wishing he was in his room and in bed. Then suddenly Harold remembered. He remembered where his bedroom window was when there was a moon. It was always right around the moon. And then Harold moved his bed. He got in it and he drew up the covers. The purple crayon dropped on the floor and Harold dropped off to sleep."
Child: (smiling)
Parent: "[crosstalk 00:19:42] Is that the end?"
Child: (nodding)
Parent: "Yes."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "You good?"
Child: (nodding)
Parent: "We read two stories. One short, one long. Right?"
Child: (stretching arms)
Parent: "Can you please take them off for me, please?"
Child: (nodding)
Parent: "Okay."
Child: (helping to remove the equipment)
Parent: "And just take this off, thank you."
Child: (looking around)
Parent: "Thank you very much."
Child: (talking to another adult)
Parent: "Mom, I’m not [crosstalk 00:20:20]"
Child: (listening)
Parent: "(Foreign Language.)"
Child: (nodding)
Parent: "Thank you."
Child: (continuing conversation)
Parent: "(Foreign Language.)"
Child: (pointing)
Parent: "Sure."
Child: (getting up)
Parent: "In the story reading activity, how did you feel?"
Child: (thinking)
Parent: "I feel..."
Child: (looking at visual aids)
Parent: "This one’s like very very happy, this one is unhappy and this one is okay and this one is unsure and a little sad, and this one is really sad."
Child: (pointing)
Parent: "In the activity, I felt nervous and wanted to go home. So this one was very very nervous and this one was very very liked relaxed."
Child: (sitting back down)
Parent: "In this activity, I felt sleepy and wanted to take a nap."
